slides.title:
She started
with *$1.25*.
She built an empire.
slides.sub:
Orphan at 7. Washerwoman at $1.50 a day.
Then she changed everything 👇

slides.title:
Sarah Breedlove is born
on a *Louisiana plantation*,
to formerly enslaved parents.
slides.sub:
By age 7, she's an orphan
(National Women's History Museum, PBS).

slides.title:
Married at 14. A widow
with a 2-year-old daughter
*by age 20*.
slides.sub:
She washes laundry for 18 years,
often for as little as $1.50 a day
(Smithsonian).

slides.title:
In the 1890s, she notices
*bald spots*. She needs
a fix for her own hair.
slides.sub:
She later said the formula came to her
in a dream. She starts mixing her own
products (PBS, Smithsonian).

slides.title:
1905, Denver: she launches
*her own hair grower*
with $1.25 in savings.
slides.sub:
She renames herself “Madam C.J. Walker”
and sells Madam Walker's Wonderful
Hair Grower (NWHM, PBS).

slides.title:
No store. No investors.
She sells *door to door*,
at churches and clubs.
slides.sub:
Then by mail order. And she trains
other women to sell for her
(PBS).

slides.title: Don't sit down and wait for the opportunities to come. *Get up and make them.*
slides.author:
Madam C.J. Walker, to her sales agents
(Smithsonian)

slides.title:
1910: her own *factory* and
beauty school in Indianapolis.
An army of “Walker Agents”.
slides.sub:
20,000-40,000 agents (Smithsonian, PBS).
Sales topped $500,000 in 1919,
her final year (NWHM).

slides.title:
Solve *your own*
problem first.
slides.sub:
She built for women like her,
then turned customers into sellers.
